boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Appomattox Court House record (April 9, 1865) in the Appomattox Campaign [March-April 1865]. The engagement of the morning and the surrender that followed are one frozen record. Humphreys commanded the Second Corps, and his account of its actions here is a participant's. Army-wide returns, campaign-wide loss and prisoner totals, the April 9 paroles and the retreat as a whole are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 'Armies' and the live field zero. Lee reported that on the morning of the 9th the ordnance officers counted 7,892 organized infantry with arms, the artillery was reduced to 63 pieces, the cavalry did not in his belief exceed 2,100 effective men, and the enemy were more than five times his numbers; Humphreys relays Fitzhugh Lee's mounted force of about 2,400 and the statement that only 8,000 of those surrendered had arms.
claims.rationale: Lee's figures are his army-wide armed strength that morning; Fitzhugh Lee's (via Humphreys) is the cavalry's mounted force at daybreak; the 8,000 is an unattributed statement. None is a count of the troops engaged. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads '700 total (27,805 Confederate soldiers paroled)' and the live field 664 (US 164; CS 500). Humphreys gives the War Department's paroles as 26,707 of infantry, cavalry and artillery and 28,356 with detachments, and the Union loss from March 29 to April 9 as 9,944 (8,268 killed and wounded and 1,676 missing).
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The parole counts are a post-surrender population on different bases from the frozen 27,805; the 9,944 is campaign-wide context and is not assigned to this record.

open_questions: Grant's report (No. 1, Richmond campaign), Meade's, Ord's, Gibbon's and Crook's reports (Nos. 4, 213, 219, 208; Gibbon's selected and cited under VA092), Gordon's and Longstreet's accounts, Fitzhugh Lee's report (selected; cited under other records), the parole table (No. 269), the Union casualty return (No. 2) and the Grant-Lee correspondence (Humphreys' Appendix M) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the commander of the Second Corps in this campaign, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; where it narrates his own corps it is a participant's account. It relies on the reports of Sheridan, Warren, Wright, Gibbon, Ewell and Fitzhugh Lee, on Confederate testimony before the Warren Court of Inquiry and on the returns, so it is not independent of those families. Lee's, Sheridan's, Bushrod Johnson's, Miles's, Gibbon's, Ewell's and Fitzhugh Lee's papers, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XLVI, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
